title: Billions of dollars and billboards failed in Solomon Islands. What changed?

Topic:Foreign Affairs

One of the many Australian government billboards in Solomon Islands' capital, Honiara. (ABC News: Chrisnrita Aumanu-Leong)

In Solomon Islands' capital Honiara, the roadside billboards are a little different.

The nation's number one rice brand Solrice is everywhere, advertising its latest deals. And Telekom, the biggest mobile phone provider, takes almost every second spot, talking about its "outrageous" data plans.

But, curiously, another entity dominates the local billboard scene: the Australian government.

About a dozen big white Australian government billboards are scattered in prime positions off the capital's main road, promoting in English and Solomon Islands pijin all the wonderful things Australia has done for the country.

Bin sapotim yufala longtaem (We've been supporting you for a long time), one of the billboards shouts. Nambawan patna long sekiuriti (Your number one security partner), proclaims another.

A billboard promotes the "Australia-Solomon Islands partnership".   (ABC News: Chrisnrita Aumanu-Leong)

Looking like they've been created in Microsoft Paint by the office intern, they're rather uninspiring; you can just imagine Todd Sampson on The Gruen Transfer rolling his eyes at the sight of them.

The billboards started popping up en masse a few years back in the aftermath of 2019's "The Switch", when Solomon Islands kicked Taiwan out of the country and embraced China, later signing a controversial security pact with Beijing.

Despite spending billions in aid over the past decade on a range of transformative projects, Australia found, with a combative leader at the helm in the form of firebrand Manasseh Sogavare, gaining any traction in the country was hard graft. The billboards are a case in point.

But it turns out Australia didn't need bland roadside advertising to push its narrative in Solomon Islands. Canberra just needed a change in leader.

In his three months as Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale has performed a full directional diplomatic twist for Solomon Islands, the type an Olympic gymnast would be proud of.

From years of panic in Canberra that China could even build a military base in the country, the ABC yesterday revealed that Australia had reached in-principle agreement with Solomon Islands on a sweeping new treaty, with Canberra committing almost a billion dollars to the Pacific nation.

Australia and Solomon Islands have reached an in-principle agreement over a new treaty.

It came just days after Wale fended off a surprise no-confidence motion, forcing him to abruptly leave the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau to save his job (and in all likelihood the treaty itself).

New Zealand's foreign affairs minister Winston Peters even suggested he was "highly suspicious" about whether foreign interference (insert China) had played a part in it all.

Solomon Islands PM and outgoing Pacific Islands Forum chair Matthew Wale makes shock departure from the PIF leaders meeting to deal with looming leadership challenge back home.

But leaving all the James Bond spy stuff for a second, a billion dollars is a lot of money, particularly as political parties such as One Nation pledge to reduce foreign aid and spending in the region.

So, it begs the question, is the Albanese government's multi-billion push in the Pacific worth it?

"Well if you look at the overall defence budget of around $60 billion annually, this [the treaty] is a massive return on investment," Pacific Islands program director at the Lowy Institute, Oliver Nobetau, said.

What Australia will get in return in the treaty has not yet been revealed, but Nobetau said the "likely" scenario would be language that cemented Australia as being the security partner of choice to eventually "shut out" countries such as China.

Solomon Islands still has a security pact with China, which Nobetau said would not be "suddenly cut off".

"Australia will need to demonstrate over time that it can be that security partner pragmatically," he said. "And over time it would want to push a shift towards it, rather than shutting the door on China."

The treaty with Solomon Islands comes on the back of a wave of activity in the region, with the Australian government spending billions to shore up support to become the region's number one security partner, in what it describes as its "permanent contest" with China.

This week, perhaps for the first time in a long time, some sections of the Pacific are signalling a slight adjustment to their relationship with China.

Treaties or agreements with Papua New Guinea (PukPuk Treaty), Fiji (Vuvale Union and the Ocean of Peace Alliance) and Vanuatu (the Nakamal Agreement) have been inked.

Then there's the Falepili Union with Tuvalu (signed in 2023) the Nauru-Australia Treaty (2024), and Canberra is also in discussions with Tonga on the Kaume ' a Ofi agreement.

Looking at a map, it's now pretty much a web of treaties across the Pacific. It's a map no doubt Beijing will be looking at with contempt.

But with its relentless push in the Pacific, its undeniable security focus and constant narrative around China, another question must be posed: Is this being well received by Pacific Islanders?

"I think Australia has got better at listening," Nobetau said.

"You can't bulldoze these agreements through and you have to listen to exactly what it is that Pacific Island countries want."

Back in Solomon Islands, the devil will be in the detail when the full treaty is made public.

But in what one commentator said showed Australia was willing to do "whatever it takes" to get the treaty over the line, we know Australia is committing $68 million for what it called MPs' "development priorities".

These "development priorities" are loosely defined, but appear to resemble the controversial constituency development funds — money given to MPs to essentially use at their discretion.

With so much scrutiny brought on China when it made a similar move, the microscope should rightly be put on this money to make sure it is used appropriately.

That pool of money is no doubt being offered to win favour from potentially sceptical local MPs and their voters, who still question Australia's motives in the country.

A billboard promotes the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.  (ABC News: Nick Sas)

And on that, if there is one topic that will undoubtedly help Australia in its quest to win favour, it is visas.

The leaked texts accessed by the ABC reveal a large sum of money for unspecified "visa improvements", a long-held bugbear of the Pacific community.

I was in Solomon Islands last month and a old friend brought this up.

He told me the Albanese government talks about the "Pacific family" as they force Pacific Islanders through a long-winded and expensive process just to come and visit Australia.

"That's what you do to family?" he said. "That's like making your uncle or auntie fill in a form, pay $200 and wait 30 days before being allowed in the house for Christmas lunch."

Either way, with the treaty looking like it will be signed in the coming weeks, one thing's for sure: those billboards in Honiara will need an upgrade soon.
